q: How many workweeks of leave can an eligible employee take under the FMLA in a 12-month period?
answer: Under the FMLA, an eligible employee working for a covered employer can take up to 12 weeks of leave in any 12-month period. This applies for reasons like your own serious health condition or caring for a spouse, child, or parent with one.

q: How many hours do I need to have worked to be eligible for FMLA leave?
answer: To be FMLA-eligible, you must have worked for your employer at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before you take leave—about 24 hours a week on average. You also need 12 months of total employment with that employer (breaks under 7 years generally still count), and you must work at a location where the employer has at least 50 employees within 75 miles.

q: How many employees does my employer need within 75 miles for me to qualify for FMLA?
answer: You need to work at a location where your employer has at least 50 employees within 75 miles of your worksite. Even if your employer has 50+ employees total, if they're spread out and fewer than 50 work within that 75-mile radius of your site, you won't be eligible for FMLA leave.

q: How much FMLA leave can I take to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness?
answer: You may take up to 26 weeks of FMLA leave in a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness.

q: Is FMLA leave paid?
answer: No. FMLA leave itself is unpaid. But if you have paid sick, vacation, or personal time saved up, you can use it during your FMLA leave so you keep getting paid, and your employer can even require you to use that paid leave. Either way, your time off stays protected as FMLA leave. In Illinois, employees on FMLA may also use Paid Leave for All Workers Act time concurrently, sometimes required by the employer.

q: Under the Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act, how many hours do I have to work to earn one hour of paid leave?
answer: Under PLAWA, you earn 1 hour of paid leave for every 40 hours you work, up to a cap of 40 hours of paid leave per 12-month period. Only hours actually worked count toward this accrual—time spent on paid leave or unpaid leave doesn't count. Employers can also choose to frontload the full 40 hours at the start of the year instead of using this accrual method.

q: In Chicago, how many hours do I need to work to earn one hour of Paid Leave?
answer: In Chicago, you earn one hour of Paid Leave for every 35 hours you work, up to a cap of 40 hours of Paid Leave per 12-month period (unless your employer sets a higher limit). You earn Paid Sick Leave at the same rate, separately.

q: I work in Chicago. How long do I have to wait before I can start using Paid Leave?
answer: If you work in Chicago, you can start using your Paid Leave on your 90th day of employment, or July 1, 2024, whichever is later. (Note: this is for Paid Leave; Paid Sick Leave under the same ordinance can be used starting on your 30th day of employment.)

q: Can I use Illinois paid leave for any reason, or do I have to say why I need it?
answer: Yes. Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act lets you take paid leave for any reason, or no reason at all. Your employer cannot ask why you want the leave or demand proof like a doctor's note for the standard 40 hours of leave. The only exception: if your employer voluntarily offers more than 40 hours of paid leave per year, they may set a reasonable, written policy requiring a reason or documentation for use of those extra hours beyond the required 40.

q: I work in Chicago. Does the Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act or the Chicago ordinance apply to me?
answer: If you work in Chicago, the Chicago Paid Leave and Paid Sick and Safe Leave Ordinance applies to you, not the state PLAWA. Chicago passed its own paid leave ordinance before January 1, 2024, so it covers employees and employers in Chicago instead of PLAWA. For questions about the Chicago rules, contact the City of Chicago Office of Labor Standards.

q: How much paid leave do I earn each year?
answer: This depends on where you work. In Illinois (outside Chicago) under PLAWA, you earn 1 hour of paid leave for every 40 hours worked, up to 40 hours total in a 12-month period [il-plawa-faq#7]. Hours used for paid or unpaid leave don't count toward accrual [il-plawa-faq#20]. If you work in Chicago, the Paid Leave Ordinance uses a different rate: you earn 1 hour of Paid Leave for every 35 hours worked [chi-paid-leave-faq#9], and you can earn up to an additional 40 hours in a year, with up to 16 hours carried over, for a possible balance of up to 56 hours [chi-paid-leave-faq#19]. Chicago also has separate Paid Sick Leave accrual. Check which jurisdiction your work location falls under to know which applies.

q: Am I eligible for FMLA leave?
answer: FMLA eligibility depends on your employer and work history. First, your employer must be covered: it has 50+ employees within 75 miles of your worksite, or it's a public agency, elementary, or secondary school. Second, you must have worked for that employer at least 12 months total (breaks over 7 years usually don't count). Third, you must have worked at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before your leave (about 24 hrs/week average). Flight crew employees have a different rule: 60% of their monthly guarantee plus at least 504 hours worked or paid in the prior 12 months. If any of these don't apply to you, you likely aren't FMLA-eligible, though you may still request leave again later if your situation changes.

q: I work part-time. Do I get paid leave?
answer: Yes, part-time workers generally earn paid leave, but details depend on where you work. In Illinois (outside Chicago), under PLAWA you earn 1 hour of paid leave per 40 hours actually worked, capped at 40 hours/year. If your employer frontloads leave instead of accrual, part-time workers get a pro-rated amount based on expected hours, not the full 40 (il-plawa-faq#20, il-plawa-faq#21). In Chicago, there's no distinction between part-time and full-time employees - you're a 'Covered Employee' once you work at least 80 hours for your employer within 120 days while physically in Chicago, and then you keep accruing leave (chi-paid-leave-faq#2). q: If I take Illinois paid leave, does it count against my FMLA leave too?
answer: It depends on whether your time off also qualifies as FMLA leave. If you are taking leave for a reason that qualifies under the FMLA, your employer can have your Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act (PLAWA) time run at the same time as your FMLA leave — the sources say employees going on FMLA 'may use or may be required by their employer to use PLAWA time concurrently during their FMLA leave.' So in that case, yes, it counts against your FMLA leave. If your PLAWA leave is for a reason that doesn't qualify for FMLA, it wouldn't be FMLA leave at all, so it wouldn't reduce your FMLA entitlement. For specific FMLA eligibility or designation questions, the sources say to contact the U.S. Department of Labor.
